\begin{center}
    \Large
    \textbf{Abstract}
\end{center}

Epic abstract about the diff-in-diff effects on municipal structures on government expenditure.

\newpage

## The exam

The exam for SOK-3026 is a term paper. Students apply the Difference-in-Differences (DiD) method to analyse the impact of an economic policy or reform on an economic outcome, using publicly available panel data. The paper should follow the structure of a research article.

## Suggested topics and data sources


You may evaluate the effect of changes in municipal structure (Kommunereformen) on different outcomes. You may also propose original topics from any field of economics (health, education, trade, labour, and so on). Replications of existing studies are permitted if they use a different dataset or extend the original analysis, and if they avoid plagiarism.


## The 2014–2020 local government reform

Norway’s municipal structure changed as part of the 2014–2020 local government reform (Kommunereformen). Most mergers took effect on 1 January 2020, reducing the number of municipalities from 422 to 356. Since then activity has been limited, with no new mergers and only one notable split (in 2024). The 2020 changes involved 119 municipalities merging into 47 new ones.

Examples of indicators that might be affected by the reform are listed below. You are free to use other indicators available at ssb.no/statbank/list/kostrahoved.

## How to construct pre-2020 data for proto-municipalities

When two or more municipalities merge, the post-2020 unit is a new (or enlarged) entity. Thepre-2020 data are reported for the old, smaller municipalities. To use DiD you need one consistent unit that can be followed over time. That unit is the proto-municipality: the artificial municipality you create by aggregating the pre-2020 data of all the municipalities that later became the new entity.

In the final panel the proto-municipality and the post-2020 municipality must share the same identifier (the same id or municipality code). That is what makes the unit comparable before and after the reform. Without a common identifier the panel is broken and the DiD comparison is invalid.
 
How to aggregate:

• Totals (expenditures, number of cases, revenues, etc.): sum the values of the old municipalities.
• Per-inhabitant measures: obtain the population of each old municipality (for example from SSB Table 11805), compute the weighted average or, equivalently, sum the underlying totals and divide by the sum of the populations. Do not simply average the rates.

Example 1: Lillestrøm. Lillestrøm (knr 3201) did not exist before 2020. It was created by merging Fet (knr 0227), Skedsmo (knr 0230) and Sørum (knr 0226).

• Pre-2020: create one “proto-Lillestrøm” row per year by aggregating the three old municipalities.
• Post-2020: use the official Lillestrøm data.
• Give both the proto-rows and the post-2020 rows the same identifier (for example knr 3201).

There is no pre-2020 Lillestrøm series, so aggregation is the only way to obtain a pre-period for the treatment unit.
 
Example 2: Asker. Asker already existed before 2020 (old knr 0620). In 2020 it was enlarged by
merging with Hurum (knr 0628) and Røyken (knr 0627). The post-2020 Asker (knr 3205) therefore
covers a larger area than the old Asker.

• Pre-2020: aggregate old Asker + Hurum + Røyken into one “proto-Asker” row per year.
• Post-2020: use the official (enlarged) Asker data.
• Again, use the same identifier for the proto-rows and the post-2020 rows.

If you used only the old Asker series for the pre-period, you would be comparing a smaller geographical unit before the reform with a larger unit after the reform. That breaks the consistency of the treatment unit.

Summary of the difference.

• Lillestrøm: the post-2020 municipality is entirely new. Aggregation is required to create any pre-period at all.
• Asker: the post-2020 municipality is an enlargement of an existing one. Aggregation is still required so that the pre-period matches the post-period geographical area.

In both cases the goal is the same: one stable unit, one identifier, a clean before–after comparison.

## Important notes

• You are free to evaluate other policies.
• Include as many municipalities as possible in both treatment and control groups, because the data are aggregated at the municipality level.
• For merged municipalities, construct a consistent geographical unit (proto-municipality) for the pre-period so that the treatment unit is comparable over time.

```{r}
# Code written by ChatGPT 6.2 to complete the dataset for the diff-in-diff.
# Frozen official code lists (one row per 2020 municipality). Each period lists
# the raw codes to sum. The 2020 code is also the stable analytical ID.
# Kartverket, mapping 2019 -> 2020:
# https://kartverket.no/til-lands/kommunereform/tekniske-endringer-ved-sammenslaing-og-grensejustering/komendr2020
# Kartverket, mapping 2023 -> 2024:
# https://kartverket.no/til-lands/fakta-om-norge/norske-fylke-og-kommunar
# SSB KLASS 131, earlier changes (including Trøndelag renumbering):
# https://data.ssb.no/api/klass/v1/classifications/131/changes.json?from=2015-01-01&to=2026-01-01
# Boundary exceptions:
# https://www.ssb.no/metadata/alle-endringer-i-de-regionale-inndelingene
# Multiple outgoing destinations cannot be apportioned using municipal totals.

# Assign treatment from multiple 2019 predecessors. Sample rules are applied
# before aggregation. Code-only changes contribute one predecessor.
sample_units <- subset(crosswalk, status == "include")
sample_units$treated <- as.integer(grepl(" ", sample_units$y2019))
raw_codes <- substr(panel$region, 1, 4)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(raw_codes), all(grepl("^[0-9]{4}$", raw_codes)))
raw_names <- sub("^[0-9]{4} +", "", panel$region)
sample_units$municipality <- raw_names[match(sample_units$y2024, raw_codes)]
stopifnot(!anyNA(sample_units$municipality))

aggregate_year <- function(year) {
  period <- as.character(cut(year, breaks = c(2014, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2023, 2025),
                             labels = c("y2015", "y2017", "y2018", "y2019", "id", "y2024")))
  members <- strsplit(sample_units[[period]], " ", fixed = TRUE)
  codes <- unlist(members, use.names = FALSE)
  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(codes), all(codes %in% raw_codes))
  cost_col <- paste("Beløp (1000 kr) 120 Administrasjon Brutto driftsutgifter på funksjon/tjenesteområde", year)
  pop_col <- paste("Personer (antall)", year, "I alt")
  stopifnot(all(c(cost_col, pop_col) %in% names(panel)))
  rows <- lapply(members, match, table = raw_codes)
  # A missing constituent makes the corresponding total missing.
  sum_members <- function(column) {
    vapply(rows, function(i) sum(panel[[column]][i]), numeric(1))
  }
  cost <- sum_members(cost_col)
  population <- sum_members(pop_col)
  stopifnot(all(population > 0, na.rm = TRUE))
  data.frame(
    id = sample_units$id, municipality = sample_units$municipality, year = year,
    treated = sample_units$treated, post = as.integer(year >= 2020),
    did = sample_units$treated * as.integer(year >= 2020), event_time = year - 2020L,
    admin_1000nok = cost, population = population,
    admin_nok_pc = 1000 * cost / population,
    source_codes = sample_units[[period]]
  )
}

panel_all <- do.call(rbind, lapply(2015:2025, aggregate_year))
missing_years <- subset(panel_all, is.na(admin_1000nok) | is.na(population))
# Keep all usable municipality-years. Missing values never become zero.
df_did <- subset(panel_all, !is.na(admin_nok_pc))
df_did <- df_did[order(df_did$id, df_did$year), ]
row.names(df_did) <- NULL
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(df_did[c("id", "year")]))
excluded <- subset(crosswalk, status != "include")
#print(with(df_did, table(year, treated)))


# Optional: estimates in current NOK per inhabitant, clustered by stable unit.

# save the panel data as excel file
wb <- createWorkbook()
addWorksheet(wb, "panel_data")
writeData(wb, sheet = "panel_data", df_did)
saveWorkbook(wb, "dokumentobjekter/data/final_data.xlsx", overwrite = TRUE)

```


# Introduction

The Norwegian municipal reform of 2020 reduced the number of municipalities from 422 to 356. The reform was motivated by the idea that larger municipalities can provide better services at lower cost. One potential source of savings is administrative spending, which may be reduced when several municipalities share management teams, payroll systems and other functions. This paper examines whether administrative spending per resident declined in merged municipalities relative to unchanged municipalities after the reform.


## Background

Lets open with a concrete budget question. When several municipalities merge, they may be able to reduce administrative costs by sharing resources and functions. However, the transition period can be costly as the merged entity needs to integrate the systems and staff of the predecessor municipalities. What is the net effect on administrative spending per resident? The cost per resident is a relevant measure because it accounts for the size of the population served by the municipality. A reduction in administrative spending per resident could indicate that the merged municipality is operating more efficiently, while an increase could suggest that the transition costs are outweighing any potential savings.


## Research question

How did gross administrative spending per resident change in Norwegian municipalities that merged on 1 January 2020, relative to municipalities with stable boundaries? Annual data from 2015 to 2025 allow us to examine the timing of any change in administrative spending per resident before and after the reform. This can allow us to assess whether the reform had a lasting effect on administrative efficiency or whether any observed changes were temporary.

## Policy Context

# Literature review

## Danish evidence

Municipal mergers may reduce the cost of administration because several municipalities can share management team, payroll system and other functions before maintained separately. Evidence from Denmark support this argument. Using the Danish reform in 2007 to compare merged and unchanged municipalities, @blom2014size found that mergers lowered adimistrative costs per inhabitant. Later @blom2016jurisdiction did a broader analysis of the same reform, and found that savings in some spending areas were offset by increases elsewhere. Together, these findings explain why the choice of outcome can matter. A municipality could spend less on administration and redirect those resources to local services while its total expenditure remains unchanged. Our study focuses on administrative spending per resident, which is a relevant measure of efficiency in the context of municipal mergers.

## Norwegian context

In Norway, an important question is when spending begins to change. @askim2025local found that municipalities increased their spending in current expenditure. Their study examines broader spending categories, leaving open whether the same pattern occured in the administration. This could matter for our analysis because an unusually high level of spending in 2019 could make a post-2020 reduction appear larger than it really is. We therefore examine the timing of any change in administrative spending per resident.

The Danish studies provide a benchmark for administrative savings, while the Norwegian evidence raises a question about spending before implementation. We bring these questions together by following the 2020 Norwegian merger cohort through 2025.


# Brief theory framework

The scope for administrative savings depends on which costs can be shared and how quickly they can be adjusted. A merged municipality can operate one payroll system for the combined population, but it may initially have to maintain both existing systems while transferring records and training staff. Therefore transition costs could raise spending during preparation, while reductions in duplicated functions could appear over several years. Gradual staff turnover may also delay changes in wage expenditure. We therefore expect any reduction in administrative spending per resident to be more visible several years after a merger than in its first year. The size and timing of that change are our empirical questions.


# Data

## Sources

The data come from Statistics Norway (SSB) and the Norwegian Mapping Authority (Kartverket). SSB provides annual data for gross operating expenditure on function 120 (municipal consolidated accounts, thousand NOK) at [table 12362](https://www.ssb.no/en/statbank/table/12362) and for total population on 31 December (persons) at [table 11805](https://www.ssb.no/en/statbank/table/11805), while Kartverket provides information on municipal boundaries and mergers. We use these sources to construct a panel dataset of Norwegian municipalities from 2015 to 2025, including both merged and unchanged municipalities.

# Estimated results

```{r}
model <- fixest::feols(
  admin_nok_pc ~ did | id + year,
  data = df_did,
  vcov = ~id
)

summary(model)
```

## Diff-in-diff estimates

```{r}
df_did |>
  mutate(group = if_else(treated == 1, "Merged in 2020", "Control")) |>
  group_by(year, group) |>
  summarise(mean_spending = mean(admin_nok_pc), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, mean_spending, colour = group)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2019.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2025) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Administrative spending (NOK per resident)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```
```{r}
# Does the 2019 peak drive the main result?
model_no_2019 <- fixest::feols(
  admin_nok_pc ~ did | id + year,
  data = subset(df_did, year != 2019),
  vcov = ~id
)

# Did spending grow at different rates before the mergers?
model_pretrend <- fixest::feols(
  admin_nok_pc ~ treated:I(year - 2015) | id + year,
  data = subset(df_did, year < 2020),
  vcov = ~id
)

fixest::etable(model, model_no_2019, model_pretrend)
```

## Robust checks (if relevant)

# Discussion

Administrative spending per resident declined in merged municipalities relative to controls after 2020. The estimated reduction was similar when we excluded 2019. However, spending in the two groups was already evolving differently before the reform, which limits the casual interpretation of the estimated reduction. The results are consistent with the idea that merged municipalities can share administrative costs, but they also suggest that other factors may have contributed to the observed changes in spending

\section{Appendix General AI Use}

When I write code in Visual Studio Code or RStudio, I use a plugin called GitHub Copilot. This plugin will try to suggest code or sentences(even paragraphs) as I write. I sometimes accept the suggestions but only if it's how I would do it. There are also cases where it can be seen in the code that I comment with a "plotting year on x, value on y" so that it will just autofill the code we usually use.

Documenting each of these instances would be cumbersome and wouldn't serve any purpose. All code sections with such comments can be assumed to have involved GitHub Copilot. More information about this AI tool is available at <https://github.com/features/copilot>.

Doing coding has changed over the last few years, and ChatGPT 6.2 was used to help with merging the data and creating the panel dataset. The code was written in R and is available in the appendix, the code chunks is labeled as such. It was reviewed by me to ensure that it was correct and appropriate for the analysis.
